title: Japanese Team Develops Chip to Detect Signs of Extraterrestrial Life
site_name: BGNES: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
excerpt: An international team led by researchers at the University of Osaka in Japan has developed a new electrical method for detecting potential signs of life beyond Earth, ScienceAlert reports. Publishe
content:
The method has been tested on samples from the Murchison meteorite and Chile’s Atacama Desert, producing results comparable to those of conventional techniques

An international team led by researchers at the University of Osaka in Japan has developed a new electrical method for detecting potential signs of life beyond Earth, ScienceAlert reports. Published in Nature Communications, the technique focuses on amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and promises to offer a simpler alternative to existing approaches.

Amino acids exist in two mirror-image forms, known as L and D. The balance between them in a sample can provide clues as to whether the molecules originated from living organisms or non-biological processes. The new method detects this property, known as chirality, using a tiny gap between two gold nanowires. An electrical tunnelling current flows across the gap through a quantum mechanical effect that allows electrons to pass between the wires.

When a solution containing amino acid molecules is applied to the device, the current changes in measurable ways, revealing which form the amino acids take. Machine-learning algorithms then distinguish between the L and D forms by analysing the electrical signals.

“By combining our nanogap tunnelling technique with artificial intelligence, we were able to distinguish between the L- and D-forms of amino acids with over 80% accuracy. This is the first discrimination of amino-acid chirality at the single-molecule level,” says Takahito Ohshiro, a bioengineer at the University of Osaka.

The researchers say the conventional approach, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), requires bulky equipment, relatively large samples and multiple chemical processing steps, making it unsuitable for use aboard a lunar rover.

The team has already tested the new approach on natural samples from the Murchison meteorite in Australia and soil collected from Chile’s Atacama Desert.

“Our method was comparable to traditional methods, as both were capable of capturing the major features of amino acid composition,” says nanotechnology researcher Masateru Taniguchi.

The device is not a remote detector capable of identifying extraterrestrial life from a distance. Samples would still need to be collected and analysed. However, its compact design and reduced sample-preparation requirements mean it could eventually be carried aboard robotic probes and rovers exploring distant moons and planets in search of potential signs of life.

One of the next challenges, according to the researchers, will be preparing the sensor to recognise molecules it has not previously encountered or been trained to identify. The technology could be developed further for chemical analysis both on Earth and beyond it. | BGNES
